findings.where: The last section, "Hostelworld, for comparison" (desktop-02 and desktop-03, phone-02)
findings.fault: The page names Hostelworld in a heading and gives a paragraph to how Hostelworld's scores fall short, ending with how a small hostel "can look thin there". The brief says Manta must never compete with Hostelworld and that its claims name no competitor. So the page closes by attacking a competitor when it should close on Manta's own method.
findings.who_objects: The founder, because the Hostelworld affiliate application is still waiting on the cl. 6.1(c) consent request (#78), and the positioning says not to name competitors. A backpacker might object too: a method page that ends by knocking a rival reads like marketing rather than an open, neutral explanation, and that weakens the trust the page is meant to build.

findings.where: The intro paragraph under "How we rank", compared with the "Ranking method" and "Scoring method" sections
findings.fault: The intro says the page "states it in full", but the method stays vague in the places a sceptic would check. It never says what the "information on record" behind rank is, or what order results appear in. It doesn't define "area" or how the area average is worked out. "Our checks" and "approval checks" are never explained. How much the area average pulls is given only as "a handful" and "a few dozen" reviews. Decay is given only at three points, with no rule for the months in between. The heading promises something the page doesn't deliver.
findings.who_objects: A hostel owner reached by cold outreach, who reads this page to learn how their property will be placed and can't work it out. A careful traveller will also notice that a page claiming to be "in full" still leaves the key inputs vague, so the openness reads as only partial.

findings.where: The page as a whole: the header area under "How we rank" and the footer
findings.fault: Nothing says who runs Manta or who stands behind these promises. The only sign of a person is the luc@ email address in the footer. The method also has no date, no 'last updated' line and no version number. The only date on the page belongs to the Hostelworld citation. A visitor can't tell whether this is the method in use today, or who answers for it.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor deciding whether to believe that "no hostel can pay for a higher position". A promise like that is only as good as the person or company making it, and a published method needs a date for anyone to check it against what the site does. Hostel owners weighing a cold approach from an unknown pre-launch platform feel this most.

findings.where: The end of the page, after the last section (desktop-02 to desktop-03, phone-02)
findings.fault: The page stops with no next step. There's no link to browse hostels or destinations, and nothing for an owner such as how to list a property or get in touch about the method. On a phone, the only way on is to scroll back to the top and open Menu. A visitor this page has just won over is left at a dead end.
findings.who_objects: The backpacker on a phone, often mid-transit, who opened this page to decide whether to trust the rankings and now has to work out how to get back to them. Also the founder, who loses the visitors at the moment they are most convinced.

findings.where: The whole page: the long paragraphs under "Ranking method" and "Scoring method", and the "How we rank" header area, which has nothing loud in it
findings.fault: The page reads like a terms-of-service document. It is several screens of dense, legal-sounding prose ("The one count where a hostel's listing changes is zero"), with no illustration and no sign of the beachy brand voice. The brief names sterile and corporate as the enemy and wants a loud claim with plain mechanics beneath it. Here the claim ("No hostel can pay for a higher position") is just the first item in a small numbered list.
findings.who_objects: The brand owner, because the brand sheet says effortless should be the first feeling and a loud claim should sit above plain mechanics. The backpacker on a phone also gets about four screens of fine print and is likely to stop reading before the parts that would earn their trust.
